headline: The lab of Nobel Prize-winning chemist David Baker has used a new AI model, RFdiffusion3, to design working enzymes from scratch by placing individual atoms.
score_reason: Peer-reviewed advance from a leading lab with lab-tested results, but modest activity and no medical use yet.
importance_line: Researchers in pollution clean-up and disease research gain a design tool, but the designs work only in the lab and the best protease is at the low end of natural enzyme efficiency.
summary: Chinese science news account Academic Headline, as republished by 36Kr, reports that a study in the journal Science describes RFdiffusion3, which designed an enzyme that breaks down toxic organophosphorus compounds (chemicals used in pesticides) and proteases (proteins that cut other proteins) aimed at a peptide linked to the disease amyloidosis. In lab tests, 4 of the first 96 enzyme designs were active, but the report stresses this does not show any treatment for amyloid deposits in people.
notes: Full text from fulltext file; paper date not stated.
